title: 8 Mile
full_review:
"8 Mile" (Universal) is a raw foray into the high-stakes world of Detroit's hip-hop subculture.

Directed by Academy Award winner Curtis Hanson ("L.A. Confidential"), the film revolves around Jimmy Smith Jr. (Eminem), an emotional tinderbox with a flair for street rhyme bordering on genius. Unfortunately, despite the controversial rap phenom's strong debut and a unique stratum of American culture rarely explored, the hackneyed story line lends little originality to the tired genre of inner-city angst films. Several sequences of this "Rocky" with rap rise above the cliche-laden script, but predictable plotting diminishes the movie.

Set in Detroit in 1995, much of the picture's emotional energy is symbolically fueled by 8 Mile Road, an artery cutting through the psyche of the Motor City, dividing city from suburb, white from black, success from failure. Straddling these two polarities is the volatile Jimmy. Both he and his working-class neighborhood have seen better days. Yet under the detritus, each is nourished by a wellspring of creativity. For Jimmy, it's finding expression in hip-hop music.

To Jimmy and his "crew," hip-hop/rap represents more than clever wordplay; it is an emotional life preserver, a means to not only express life's hard realities, but to rise above their dead-end existence. Much of the action is played out against the high-octane backdrop of Detroit's hip-hop clubs where the city's best rappers compete in mythic duels, wielding words like weapons, vying for the respect of their peers. To the combatants, these frenetic battles of wit are a blood-sport, each invective rhyme hurled with deadly intent.

Struggling with turbulent personal relations and chasing dreams of "making the big deal," Jimmy puts it all on the line. Channeling his rage into his music, he enters the arena in an effort to escape his downward-spiraling life and find redemption. Like Sylvester Stallone's Rocky, Jimmy yearns to go the distance with the champ, if for no other reason than to prove that he is not just another bum from the neighborhood.

Though consistent with the world chosen by the filmmaker to explore, violence is the all-too-common currency of "8 Mile," liberally doled out in equal measure with fists and words. Obscenities seem to punctuate every line of dialogue. The film's depictions of sex are more than a bit off-putting -- ranging from utilitarian (Jimmy's mom engaging in sex with her abusive live-in lover, a young man half her age, for rent money) to the recreational (Jimmy having sex with a girl he barely knows as a momentary respite from the ennui of his daily grind). Most disturbing is the representation (or absence) of parental figures. Jimmy's mother (a less than stellar performance by Kim Basinger) is pathetic at best, devoid of any moral fortitude worth emulating. Family life is portrayed as something to escape from.

Eminem, however, brings a refreshingly unpolished authenticity to his performance. While admittedly playing himself (though he contends the film is only thematically autobiographical), he possesses an untamed magnetism that injects a dangerous unpredictability into an otherwise cliche-heavy role. He also achieves moments of genuine tenderness, though far too few to invest much emotion, as audiences did with Stallone's sympathetic southpaw in "Rocky."

Curtis Hanson succeeds on one level: making the hip-hop subculture intriguing to a wider audience that might not have any interest in rap music. Mexican-born cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto also captures the gritty texture of life on Detroit's mean streets, but the explicit sex and violence coupled with constant abusive language put the film over the top.

Due to excessive violence, graphic sexual encounters, crude sexual references and continual rough language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. 2002
